content: Taxonomic rank refers to the hierarchical level of a taxon within the system of scientific classification, or taxonomy, of organisms. It is an abstract concept used to organize and categorize living organisms based on shared characteristics. Taxa at the same rank represent groupings of organisms that are classified at an equivalent level in the taxonomic hierarchy. Carl Linnaeus introduced the Linnaean taxonomy, which originally included ranks such as kingdom, class, order, genus, species, and variety. Modern taxonomy has expanded this system to include eight primary ranks: domain, kingdom, phylum (or division), class, order, family, genus, and species. However, there are slight differences in the ranks used for zoology and botany. The species rank is the most fundamental in taxonomy. When an organism is named, it is typically assigned a species name. The genus rank is the next most significant, as the genus name forms part of the species name. For example, in the binomial name Homo sapiens, Homo represents the genus, and sapiens specifies the species. The family rank, though not used by Linnaeus, is also important in modern taxonomy. Binomial names, such as Homo sapiens, are italicized when typed and underlined when handwritten. The genus name is always capitalized, while the species name is written in lowercase. In zoology, the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature defines specific taxonomic ranks, including superfamily, family, subfamily, tribe, subtribe, genus, subgenus, species, and subspecies. These ranks are grouped into family-group names, genus-group names, and species-group names. The Code governs the ranks from superfamily to subspecies but does not regulate ranks above the superfamily level. Additional unofficial ranks, such as species group, species subgroup, and species complex, are sometimes used for convenience in taxa with numerous species, such as the genus Drosophila. Lower-level taxa may also include prefixes like infrato denote subdivisions, such as infraspecies or infrasubspecies. Zoological taxa are named according to their rank. Taxa above the species level receive a uninominal (single-part) name. Species are given binomial names, consisting of a generic name and a specific name (e.g., Panthera leo for the lion). Subspecies are assigned trinominal names, which include the generic name, specific name, and subspecific name (e.g., Felis silvestris catus for the domestic cat). In botany, the International Code of Botanical Nomenclature defines a broader range of taxonomic ranks, including kingdom, subkingdom, division (or phylum), subdivision (or subphylum), class, subclass, order, suborder, family, subfamily, tribe, subtribe, genus, subgenus, section, subsection, series, subseries, species, subspecies, variety, subvariety, form, and subform. The most important ranks are kingdom, division (or phylum), class, order, family, genus, and species. Secondary ranks include tribe, section, series, variety, and form. Botanical names follow a similar structure to zoological names, with taxa at the genus level and above receiving unitary names, species-level taxa receiving binary names, and taxa below the species level receiving ternary names. For cultivated plants, additional ranks such as cultivar group and cultivar are defined under the International Code of Nomenclature for Cultivated Plants. Hybrid taxa are named using the same ranks, preceded by the prefix notho-, with nothogenus being the highest permitted rank. Examples of taxonomic classification include: The fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), commonly used in genetics research. Humans (Homo sapiens). The garden pea (Pisum sativum), used by Gregor Mendel in his genetic experiments. The fly agaric mushroom (Amanita muscaria). The bacterium Escherichia coli. Taxonomic ranks are subject to revision as new information about evolutionary relationships becomes available. For instance, the traditional classification of primates has been modified based on updated phylogenetic data. Within species, further subdivisions such as subspecies, varieties, or strains may be recognized. For example, modern humans are classified as Homo sapiens sapiens, while the garden pea is classified as Pisum sativum subsp. sativum or Pisum sativum var. macrocarpon (snow pea). Taxonomic names above the genus level are often derived from the type genus, with standard suffixes depending on the kingdom, phylum, or class. For example, the family Rosaceae is named after the genus Rosa, with the suffix -aceae indicating a family in botany. In zoology, standard suffixes are used up to the rank of superfamily. Informal ranks, such as epifamily or infrafamily, may be used to address complex phylogenetic relationships but are not regulated by the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature.
